options.text: Few-shot examples showing the agent verifying identity first and escalating a $750 refund.
options.comment: Demonstrations shape behaviour probabilistically: an agent that has been shown the right sequence can still depart from it, and no example is evaluated against the arguments of the call actually being made.

options.text: A programmatic prerequisite that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
options.comment: both are enforcement in code, evaluated on the actual call and its actual arguments. Prerequisite gates and tool-call interception hooks are the two mechanisms the guide names for deterministic compliance (Tasks 1.4 and 1.5).

options.text: A hook that intercepts the outgoing refund call, blocks amounts above $500, and redirects to escalation.
options.comment: both are enforcement in code, evaluated on the actual call and its actual arguments. Prerequisite gates and tool-call interception hooks are the two mechanisms the guide names for deterministic compliance (Tasks 1.4 and 1.5).

options.text: A system prompt stating that verification is mandatory and that refunds above $500 must be escalated.
options.comment: An instruction shapes behaviour probabilistically too. It lowers the failure rate without making it zero, and "every single time" is the stated requirement.

options.text: A nightly audit that flags any refund issued without a prior verification call.
options.comment: Detects violations after the money has moved. Detection is not prevention.

stem: A drafting agent produces long documents. Your display code shows the API response to the user whenever content holds a text block. On one long document the response cuts off mid-sentence, yet the code still presents it as the finished draft. Inspecting the response, stop_reason is "max_tokens".
question: What does that value mean, and what should the display code check before treating a response as final?

options.text: The response is complete; "max_tokens" caps the size of the request being sent, not the length of the output.
options.comment: Reverses cause and effect: the output token budget is exactly why this value was returned.

options.text: The token budget ran out mid-generation; only "end_turn" means the response is complete.
options.comment: stop_reason distinguishes several reasons generation stopped, and only "end_turn" marks a natural, complete stopping point. "max_tokens" means the output budget ran out mid-generation — the presence of a text block in content says nothing about whether that text is the whole answer. Scope note: among stop reasons, the exam guide names only the pair that drives the agentic loop, and that loop is what the task this sheet prepares tests. "max_tokens", "refusal" and "pause_turn" come from the API reference — D0 prerequisite material, not extra exam surface.

options.text: The model refused to continue for safety reasons, so nothing should be shown and the attempt should be escalated for human review instead.
options.comment: Describes "refusal", a distinct value with a distinct cause. Nothing was refused here, so withholding the draft and escalating would stall a run that only needs continuing.

options.text: A server-side tool call was interrupted mid-turn, so resending the same request unchanged lets the paused turn pick up where it left off.
options.comment: Describes "pause_turn", which concerns an interrupted server tool, not an exhausted token budget. Nothing is paused waiting to resume, so an identical resend would simply regenerate the same truncated draft.

stem: An HR assistant exposes search_policy_doc ("Retrieves policy content") and search_payroll_record ("Retrieves payroll data"). Both accept employee identifiers of a similar shape, and the model routinely picks the wrong one.
question: Which part of a tool definition drives that choice?

options.text: The position of each tool in the request's tools array.
options.comment: Declaration order is not a selection criterion.

options.text: The tool name, which outranks the rest of the definition.
options.comment: The name helps, but it cannot carry input formats, edge cases or usage boundaries.

options.text: The description, which is the primary selection mechanism.
options.comment: the model selects a tool by reading the definitions, and the description is where the meaning lives. Two one-line descriptions give it nothing to tell the tools apart, so misrouting becomes structural. The fix is to state input formats, example requests, edge cases and the boundary with neighboring tools.

options.text: The size of the input_schema: the model prefers the simplest one.
options.comment: The schema describes the arguments once a tool has been chosen; it does not decide which tool to choose.

stem: A build pipeline drives Claude across several requests. From one request to the next, a tool_result produced earlier is no longer visible to the model.
question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The API keeps no state, and the caller did not resend the earlier tool_result blocks.
options.comment: nothing carries over between requests. Every call must ship the complete messages array, tool results included; rebuilding that history is the caller's job. The same rule is what forces you to pass context explicitly to a spawned subagent.

options.text: A tool_result block expires server-side soon after it is submitted, so later requests miss it.
options.comment: Nothing expires server-side, because nothing is stored there.

options.text: The max_tokens value is too low to hold the tool_result, so the oldest blocks drop first.
options.comment: That budget bounds the output length, not the size of the history you send; and no block is dropped for you, because none is kept for you.

options.text: A session_id parameter is missing, so the server cannot attach this request to the earlier turn.
options.comment: The Messages API has no such parameter.

stem: A greenhouse operations assistant opens its system prompt with "Every answer must reflect the current sensor readings." Logs show read_sensors firing on each turn, including when a grower asks how a cultivar name should be spelled in the planting log. Each tool definition spells out its inputs and where its job ends.
question: What stops the needless calls?

options.text: Add few-shot examples of clerical turns answered without any sensor call, so the assistant can copy the pattern on the next spelling question.
options.comment: Examples cannot outvote a rule that still admits no exception; the model treats them as odd cases rather than as the boundary.

options.text: Have the client drop read_sensors from the tools array whenever it judges the incoming question clerical.
options.comment: Moves the decision to the caller, which must now classify a question before the model has read it, and leaves the misleading rule in place.

options.text: Name the conditions that call for a reading, and retire the absolute sentence.
options.comment: "every answer" reads as a permanent trigger, and the model binds it to whichever tool the wording resembles most. A rule phrased with no exceptions outranks the tool definitions, however careful they are — which is why the scenario tells you those definitions are sound. Spelling out the situations that genuinely need a reading removes the trigger while keeping the check where it earns its cost.

options.text: Cache the last reading for ten minutes so repeat turns reuse it instead of calling out again.
options.comment: Cheaper calls, identical behavior: a spelling question still travels through the sensor path, and a stale value is the wrong answer where readings matter.

stem: A ticket-triage client runs its own loop: send the request, run whatever tool comes back, append the result, send again. To stop the assistant from chatting while work remains, the client sets tool_choice to the value that guarantees a call — and it sets it on every request of the loop. Runs now end only when the client's iteration cap trips, and no written answer ever arrives.
question: Why does the run never reach one?

options.text: That value binds the first request alone; the later ones revert to the automatic setting, so the assistant keeps reaching for lookup_account long after the answer is available.
options.comment: The field is read afresh on each request; it neither expires nor decays, and the loop here restates it every time.

options.text: Each tool result is appended as a user turn, and a request whose last turn came from the user can only be answered by another call.
options.comment: A user turn carrying a tool result can be answered in prose just as readily as with another call — that is precisely what the automatic setting permits.

options.text: Repeating that value on every request removes the assistant's only way of finishing, which is a turn that ends in text; the client should guarantee the opening call and leave the remaining requests on the automatic setting.
options.comment: tool_choice: "any" promises exactly one thing, on every request that carries it: a tool will be called. Sent once, that pins the opening step. Sent on every request, it also outlaws the closing one, since a turn answering in prose is no longer permitted. Handing the later requests back to tool_choice: "auto" restores the choice between calling again and answering.

options.text: The iteration cap sits below the number of declared tools, so the client cuts the run short before classify_ticket and its neighbours have all been tried.
options.comment: The cap is what halts a run that would otherwise not halt at all; raising it buys further calls, never a written answer.

stem: An invoice extraction tool lists discount_pct among its required properties, yet plenty of invoices grant no discount. Reviewers keep finding discount figures that appear nowhere on the invoice.
question: What is happening, and what removes the cause?

options.text: The API validates the payload against the schema and rejects the call as invalid, so nothing reaches the pipeline.
options.comment: Validation covers schema conformance, never truthfulness: an invented number conforms perfectly.

options.text: The model invents a figure to satisfy the constraint; make the property nullable and no longer mandatory.
options.comment: a mandatory property leaves the model choosing between breaking the schema and making something up, and it makes something up. Declaring it "type": ["number", "null"] and taking it out of required gives the model an honest way to report absence.

options.text: The model leaves the property empty, and the pipeline should read an empty value as absent.
options.comment: Nothing empties the property while the schema still demands a value.

options.text: The model skips the tool call whenever a mandatory property has no source value.
options.comment: The tool does get called; it is the payload that is wrong.

stem: A pharmacy agent fills prescription requests through MCP tools (check_interactions, dispense, page_pharmacist). Reviewers pulled last month's transcripts and found doses released to patients whose interaction check never ran: in those requests the agent took the allergy list pasted into the ticket at face value and went straight to dispense.
question: Which change makes the skipped check impossible?

options.text: Have the agent write out the sequence it intends to follow before its first call, so a skipped step shows up in the transcript.
options.comment: A stated plan is still the model's own output, nothing holds it to what it wrote, and the transcript gets read after the dose is out.

options.text: Cache interaction results per patient so the check costs almost nothing and the agent has no reason to route around it.
options.comment: Cost was never the obstacle — the agent skipped a step it believed it already had the answer to.

options.text: Refuse dispense in code until check_interactions has returned for that patient.
options.comment: an ordering that guards a patient-safety boundary needs a guarantee, not a tendency. A prerequisite evaluated in code cannot be argued out of by a convincing-looking allergy list sitting in the ticket.

options.text: Add a hook that rejects malformed prescription identifiers before the outgoing call leaves the agent.
options.comment: Enforces a property of the arguments, not the fact that anything ran first. A well-formed identifier says nothing about the check.

stem: A coordinator was asked for a pre-launch risk brief on a payments feature. The request names five areas to cover: regulatory exposure, fraud, support load, vendor dependencies, data residency. It mentions chargebacks once, as an example under fraud. Six workers ran over two rounds and each returned a well-formed section; the brief that came back is forty pages, all of them about chargebacks. The coordinator's plan is still in the log, and it opens by restating the job as chargeback exposure.
question: Which change keeps this from recurring?

options.text: Gate the delivery step: hold the brief back until every area named in the request has a section of its own, and send the job round again whenever one of them is missing.
options.comment: The gate proves the brief incomplete only once six workers have been paid for, and it hands the job back to the same planning step that read five areas as one — so the next round can return just as narrow.

options.text: Split the work into five independent runs, one per area, and have the requester stitch the five briefs together afterwards.
options.comment: Guarantees the coverage by removing the coordinator from the job. Whatever sits across two areas is lost, and the requester now does the merging on every request.

options.text: Have the coordinator derive one assignment per area named in the request, before it delegates.
options.comment: the plan in the log names the defect — a five-part request became a one-part job before any worker started. Coverage that was never assigned cannot be recovered by anything downstream, so the fix has to sit ahead of the delegation.

options.text: Raise the worker count so each round covers more ground.
options.comment: Capacity was never the constraint. Six workers already produced forty pages; more of them widen nothing while every assignment points at the same area.

stem: Each quarter you audit the same six connector adapters against the same three concerns: retry policy, secret handling, schema versioning. Separately, you must make an undocumented ingestion pipeline observable; nobody knows how many stages it has or which already emit metrics.
question: Which strategy fits each item?

options.text: Prompt chaining for the audit, dynamic adaptive decomposition for the observability work.
options.comment: the criterion is whether the scope is known before you start. The audit repeats a fixed set of targets, so a chained sequence of focused passes gives even depth and comparable results. The observability work is open-ended: each stage you uncover changes what to look at next.

options.text: Dynamic adaptive decomposition for the audit, prompt chaining for the observability work.
options.comment: Inverts the criterion: the fixed sequence lands on the item whose steps nobody knows, the adaptive one on the item that never varies.

options.text: Prompt chaining for both, because a fixed pipeline is always more reproducible.
options.comment: A fixed pipeline presupposes knowing the stages and their order, precisely the unknown here.

options.text: Dynamic adaptive decomposition for both, because letting the model replan is always safer.
options.comment: Adaptivity buys nothing once targets are frozen, and it makes successive audits harder to compare.

stem: A migration agent needs to run read_schema, then plan_changes, then apply_migration for each table. To keep the process predictable, the orchestrator pre-computes this exact call sequence before the first request and feeds each tool result into the next hardcoded step, never letting the model's own response decide what happens next. When a table turns out to need an extra validation step the sequence doesn't account for, the agent has no way to trigger it.
question: What should change about how the loop is driven?

options.text: Keep the fixed sequence, but add a fourth hardcoded step for validation, since the gap that appeared today is now a known case.
options.comment: Fixes this one gap but leaves the orchestrator guessing every future case in advance — the same limitation returns with the next table that needs something different.

options.text: Let the model choose the next action each turn from the latest tool_result, and stop when it stops requesting tools.
options.comment: a sequence fixed in advance by the orchestrator is a hardcoded decision tree — it can only be as flexible as whoever wrote it anticipated. An agentic loop is model-driven: the model reads each tool result and decides the next action itself, the loop continues for as long as it keeps requesting tools, and it ends when the model signals it is done. That is what lets it insert a step nobody hardcoded.

options.text: Run all three tools on every turn regardless of need, so the missing step is always covered and no table can slip through, accepting the wasted work as the price of completeness.
options.comment: Running every tool regardless of need does not add judgment, it just hides the missing decision behind unconditional execution — and the completeness it buys is an illusion, since it still only covers steps that were written down.

options.text: Keep the fixed sequence, but let the orchestrator retry a failed step before moving to the next one.
options.comment: A retry addresses a step failing, not a step nobody planned for.

stem: A session named fx-integration spent a long afternoon probing a currency vendor's sandbox: sample payloads, error shapes, throttling behavior. The vendor has since shipped v3 and retired v2, so every recorded response describes an endpoint that now answers 410. What that session concluded about the vendor's pagination model and its throttling window still holds.
question: How do you take the integration work forward?

options.text: Start a new session and seed it with a summary of what still holds.
options.comment: resumption pays off while the stored tool results still describe the system you are talking to. Here they describe endpoints that answer 410, so replaying them makes the agent reason about a vendor that no longer exists. A summary carries the pagination model and the throttling window forward and leaves the dead payloads behind.

options.text: Resume the session and let the agent re-probe each endpoint as it needs one, so the recorded v2 responses get corrected along the way.
options.comment: Re-probing corrects the record only where the agent happens to look; everything it does not revisit sits in context as though it were still true.

options.text: Start a new session and replay the entire v2 transcript into it, so nothing observed that afternoon is lost.
options.comment: Carries the obsolete payloads into the new session, which is the one thing a fresh start was meant to avoid.

options.text: Start a new session with only the vendor's v3 changelog.
options.comment: A changelog says what moved on the vendor's side, not what you learned. Pagination and throttling would have to be rediscovered.

stem: A retention agent trims expired records through purge_records. Policy lets it delete up to 500 rows in one call; a larger purge needs a data steward's sign-off. The rule is written in the system prompt, and last week a single call removed 40,000 rows from an audit table.
question: What makes the ceiling hold?

options.text: Give the agent a request_signoff tool, with a description telling it when a purge has grown too large to run alone.
options.comment: Offers a way out that the agent still has to choose, and the incident was precisely a case where it did not.

options.text: A hook that blocks the outgoing call when the row count passes the ceiling.
options.comment: a ceiling that must hold every time belongs in code that sees the actual argument. The hook runs before the tool does, so an oversized purge never reaches the database, and a deletion is not something an apology can undo.

options.text: State the ceiling in the tool's own description, so the limit travels with the tool wherever it is used.
options.comment: Moves the rule closer to the call site without changing its nature: it stays text the model reads, not a condition anything evaluates.

options.text: Have the agent announce the row count it is about to delete before it issues the call.
options.comment: An announcement is a claim about an intent, made by the same run that is about to ignore it.

stem: A coordinator has a clause-extraction subagent read two vendor contracts while a pricing subagent prepares a quote, and both outputs must land in one report.
question: Which two moves are correct?

options.text: Put the contract text, the clause types wanted, and the output schema into the delegation prompt itself.
options.comment: a subagent starts from an isolated context, so whatever it needs — source text, target clause types, output shape — travels in the prompt. Parallelism comes from several delegations inside one coordinator response; spread over consecutive turns they just run one after another.

options.text: Emit both delegations in one coordinator response so the subagents run at the same time.
options.comment: a subagent starts from an isolated context, so whatever it needs — source text, target clause types, output shape — travels in the prompt. Parallelism comes from several delegations inside one coordinator response; spread over consecutive turns they just run one after another.

options.text: Count on each subagent inheriting the coordinator's conversation history.
options.comment: Nothing is inherited: an isolated context is the defining property of a subagent.

options.text: Let the clause subagent hand its output straight to the pricing subagent, saving a hop.
options.comment: Every exchange goes through the hub, which keeps the run observable and error handling uniform.

options.text: Give both subagents the coordinator's whole tool set so neither is ever blocked.
options.comment: A wider tool set degrades selection reliability; each spoke gets only the tools its role needs.

stem: A storefront agent checks availability through check_stock before it confirms an order through place_order. The available field carries three meanings in one integer: a positive number is units on hand, -1 marks an item the supplier ships on request, and 0 marks a SKU the warehouse does not track. The agent treats anything that is not positive as sold out, and it has spent a month declining orders that could have been filled.
question: Where does the fix belong?

options.text: Ask the inventory team to retire the overloaded integer and publish an explicit status field, since one number carrying three meanings will mislead every consumer of that API and not only this agent.
options.comment: The right thing to fix and the wrong thing to wait for: the field belongs to another team, every existing consumer has to move with it, and orders keep being declined until that lands.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook on place_order that blocks the confirmation whenever the availability figure behind it was not positive.
options.comment: Hardens the misreading rather than removing it. The confirmations it would block are precisely the ones that should go through, and the agent is still reading the same integer.

options.text: Log every non-positive figure and review the pattern each week.
options.comment: Counts the symptom every week and changes nothing about what the model reads. The mapping is already known, which is what makes measurement the wrong instrument.

options.text: A hook that rewrites the figure into an explicit state before the model reads the result.
options.comment: the three readings are a fixed table, so applying them is a transformation and not a judgment call. A PostToolUse hook runs it on every result on the way back, which is the last moment at which the ambiguous integer can be kept out of what the model reads.

stem: a delivery assistant routes "where is my parcel" requests to find_package 38% of the time, when they belong to find_shipment. find_shipment is described as "finds a shipment and returns its details", find_package as "finds a package and returns its details" — although find_package only returns warehouse scan events.
question: what is the right fix?

options.text: Rename find_package to list_warehouse_scans and rewrite its description around the scan events.
options.comment: two near-identical descriptions leave the model nothing to discriminate on. The new name and the rewritten description finally say what that tool really returns — warehouse scan events, not a parcel location — so the functional overlap disappears at its source, where the selection decision is actually made.

options.text: Add a routing classifier that labels every request before any tool is offered.
options.comment: Over-engineering: it bypasses natural language understanding instead of repairing the ambiguity.

options.text: Add worked routing examples to the assistant system prompt, teaching the distinction by demonstration.
options.comment: Examples cost tokens on every turn and leave the ambiguous description in place.

options.text: Expand only the find_shipment description so delivery wording pulls those requests to it.
options.comment: Improving one side keeps the other just as attractive for the same requests.

stem: a reporting subagent owns execute_sql, which accepts any statement against the warehouse. Traces show it browsing information_schema and joining raw event tables instead of reading the curated reporting views.
question: what is the right fix?

stem: A recipe importer turns ingredient lines into structured quantities. Informal amounts such as "a couple of handfuls" or "a splash" come back empty or wildly wrong, and fresh phrasings appear with every new import.

options.comment: Suppresses good extractions at the same rate as bad ones.

stem: A building-permit agent routes applications to the right municipal desk. For last quarter it reports 91% correct routing over everything it handled, and the operations team wants to switch off the human check on that basis.

stem: A synthesis agent receives two readmission rates for the same procedure: 9.4% from a 2022 national registry built on claims data, and 6.1% from a 2025 hospital survey. Both sources are credible and the methods differ.

options.text: Neither figure, since reporting numbers that contradict each other would mislead the reader.
options.comment: Dropping the statistic impoverishes the report instead of qualifying the uncertainty.

options.text: Both values with full attribution, flagged as a conflict for the reader to resolve.
options.comment: conflicting statistics from credible sources get annotated, not silently resolved. Full attribution means each value travels with its source, its date and its method, and the flag reaches the coordinator as well as the reader. The dates and the methodological gap are part of the finding: a claims-based count and a self-reported survey three years apart may not even be measuring the same thing.

stem: A hardware bring-up assistant is 120 turns into debugging a prototype board and near the context limit. Turn 3 recorded the errata in the pin mapping and the supply rail the team agreed nobody would touch. The work has to continue in this session.
question: Which strategy keeps the session going without losing those two constraints?

options.text: Move the older turns into a transcript file the assistant can open when it needs them, so the window holds only recent exchanges.
options.comment: Archives the transcript whole instead of distilling anything: the errata and the rail stay buried in 120 turns of debugging, no more prominent in the file than they were in the window. Written notes earn their keep on findings someone has boiled down and goes back to read, which is a different job from keeping a standing prohibition in force.

options.text: Compress the older turns to recover budget, and hold the two constraints in a pinned block that sits outside the region the compression is allowed to rewrite.
options.comment: the session has two problems and each needs its own answer. Compression buys room; it cannot promise that any particular line survives it. Pinning the errata and the untouchable rail outside the compressed region is what guarantees they are still there at turn 200. That is the line to hold: a prohibition has to sit in the context whenever an action is chosen, because the assistant cannot look up a rail it does not know it is about to touch, while a notes file answers a question the agent knows it has.

options.text: Trim every tool result down to its closing lines as it arrives, so the window fills more slowly from here.
options.comment: Slows saturation and protects nothing: turn 3 still sits in the part that gets compressed.

options.text: Hand each remaining subsystem to its own fresh subagent, briefed on that subsystem alone, and keep only their reports in the main thread.
options.comment: Every brief that omits the untouchable rail is a subagent free to touch it.

stem: A software licensing support agent is deep into a long ticket. The renewal discount being asked for is neither allowed nor forbidden by the pricing policy, and the account lookup returns three companies sharing the same trading name.
question: Which two responses does the escalation policy require here?

options.text: Escalate on the policy gap the discount request falls into.
options.comment: policy silence on the case is a reliable trigger, because granting the discount is a commercial decision nobody delegated. Multiple matches call for a discriminating identifier — a contract number, a billing domain — never a guess: acting on the wrong company's contract is the failure that identity checks exist to prevent.

options.text: Escalate because the ticket is long and the window is filling up.
options.comment: A filling window is a technical constraint with technical remedies, not a business reason to involve a human.

options.text: Ask for a discriminating identifier before acting on any of the three accounts.
options.comment: policy silence on the case is a reliable trigger, because granting the discount is a commercial decision nobody delegated. Multiple matches call for a discriminating identifier — a contract number, a billing domain — never a guess: acting on the wrong company's contract is the failure that identity checks exist to prevent.

options.text: Pick the account with the most recent renewal, as the likeliest match.
options.comment: "Most recent renewal" is a heuristic dressed as reasoning, and it can select the wrong account just as easily.

options.text: Score the customer's tone and escalate if it reads negative.
options.comment: Tone does not correlate with case complexity, and nothing here turns on how the customer feels.

stem: Deep into an audit of a legacy inventory module, the agent answers that "stock reconciliation jobs usually follow the observer pattern", although it had located StockLedgerSync and its callers an hour earlier. The investigation has to continue on the same files.
question: Which response treats the cause?

options.text: Raise max_tokens and ask for fuller answers, so the replies have room to carry the detail that went missing.
options.comment: That parameter bounds answer length; it has no effect on what the agent still holds.

options.text: Have the agent boil its findings down into a scratchpad file it rereads, and hand verbose discovery to a subagent that returns only a summary.
options.comment: reaching for a "typical pattern" instead of the class it actually read is the signature of context degradation. The two remedies are complementary: the scratchpad holds findings the agent has already boiled down, so what the audit learned stays readable once the window no longer holds it, and a subagent that hands back a summary only keeps verbose discovery output out of the main thread in the first place.

options.text: Rerun the exploration in a clean session and carry nothing over from this one, so the window is uncluttered again.
options.comment: Starting over with no summary injected discards the audit and reproduces the same drift.

options.text: Tell the agent to concentrate on the real code it read and to cite its sources for every claim.
options.comment: An instruction cannot restore information that is no longer usable in the context.

stem: A customs pipeline extracts nine thousand declaration line items a day. Your two reviewers get through about four hundred between them, and you want that capacity spent where it changes an outcome.
question: How should review be routed?

options.text: Rank whole declarations by certainty and work down from the weakest.
options.comment: One number per declaration averages the safe fields with the doubtful one, so it queues near-perfect documents and waves a single bad field through.

options.text: Score each field on its own, and tune the cut-off on a hand-checked sample.
options.comment: field granularity spends the reviewer where the doubt is — a declaration whose only shaky value is hs_code does not need a full reread. And a cut-off means nothing until it has been set against data someone checked by hand: ground truth is what says which score level carries an error rate you can live with.

options.text: Put every declaration through a second extraction pass, and queue the ones where the two passes disagree with each other.
options.comment: Two passes of one model agree most readily where it is confidently wrong, so the queue fills with disagreements that were never the dangerous cases.

options.text: Rotate the reviewers through each field type on a fixed weekly cycle, so no part of the form goes unchecked for long.
options.comment: A calendar decides what gets looked at, and the doubtful fields wait their turn like everything else.
